prompt: A positive integer $N$ is encoded in binary. An algorithm takes $\Theta(N)$ steps. In terms of the bit length $b=\lfloor\log_2 N\rfloor+1$, how does its running time grow?

answers.explanation: For a $b$-bit positive integer, $2^{b-1}\leq N<2^b$. Thus linear time in the numeric value is exponential in the input length.
The numeric value grows with the bit length.
This confuses the numeric value N with the number of bits used to write it.
The relationship is exponential in b, not logarithmic.
The encoded value can be exponentially larger than the square of its bit length.
That is nearly linear in bit length and much smaller than N.
N is exponential, not sublinear, in its bit length.
That scales like the square root of N, whereas the algorithm takes linear time in N.
The given cost is already Θ(N) steps; there is no additional factor of b in this statement.
That scales like N squared, rather than N.
